fable.w: This section only amends authorization-of-appropriations provisions of the Juvenile Justice and Delinquency Prevention Act by changing dollar amounts and fiscal years. One might be tempted to assume the underlying Act involves state or advisory participation, but nothing in this text calls for consultation, hearings, rulemaking, advisory bodies, or rights to sue involving any party outside the federal government.

opus.w: This section only strikes and inserts fiscal-year dates and dollar figures in two funding provisions of the Juvenile Justice and Delinquency Prevention Act, extending them through fiscal year 1984. It has no comment period, hearing, advisory body, consultation with outsiders, rulemaking, or right to sue. The parent Act may involve outside parties elsewhere, but this text does not, so the answer is No.

qwen_chat.w: This section solely amends appropriation levels and fiscal year dates for the Juvenile Justice and Delinquency Prevention Act. It does not establish any process for consulting with or coordinating with parties outside the federal government, such as the public, states, or experts. The changes are purely administrative and financial, involving only federal legislative and executive actors.
qwen_chat.s: Section 261(a) of the Juvenile Justice and Delinquency Prevention Act of 1974 (42 U.S.C. 5671(a)) is amended— (1) by striking out “$150,000,000” and all that follows through “1979, and”; and (2) by striking out “Tor the fiscal year ending September 30, 1980” and inserting in lieu thereof “Tor each of the fiscal years ending September 30, 1981, September 30, 1982, September 30, 1983, and September 30, 1984.”.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that because the statute amends a law related to juvenile justice, it implicitly involves public participation or consultation. However, the text itself only changes dollar amounts and dates for appropriations. There is no mention of hearings, comments, advisory boards, or consultation with outside parties. The actors involved are Congress (appropriating funds) and the executive branch (administering the act), all of which are inside the federal government.
